did.unittitle: African Methodist Episcopal (A.M.E.) Zion Church collection
did.abstract: Papers documenting the financial and administrative affairs of the African Methodist Episcopal (A.M.E.) Zion Church, one of Brooklyn's oldest African American congregations, organized between 1827 and 1835.

acqinfo.p: Purchase from Waiting for Godot Books, January 1999.

arrangement.p: The collection is arranged in 5 folders, each in chronological order, as follows.

bioghist.head: Historical note
bioghist.p: The A.M.E. Zion Church of Williamsburgh was located on North Second Street near Union Avenue, one of the borough's first neighborhoods inhabited in sizeable numbers by African Americans freed when New York State abolished slavery in 1827. Williamsburgh was a separate village, then a city, until it consolidated with Brooklyn in 1854.

The A.M.E. Zion Churches were a nationwide league of congregations founded in New York in 1820 by and for the African American religious community. Like the related, but separate, A.M.E. Churches, they were established and patronized by black Methodists who withdrew from the white-dominated Methodist churches as a reaction to the racism of the majority white Methodist community and to its reticence to take an organized stand against slavery as a religious issue. Members of the A.M.E. Zion Churches were actively involved in abolition work and were widely rumored to have used some of their church locations as covert Underground Railroad stations. The A.M.E. Zion Churches were progressive in other ways as well: in 1891, the A.M.E. Zion Church became one of the first major denominations to ordain women. Noted members of the nationwide A.M.E. Zion Churches included Sojourner Truth, Harriet Tubman, Jermain Loguen, and Frederick Douglass.

In 1885, Brooklyn's original A.M.E. Zion Church merged with a nearby congregation, the First A.M.E. Zion Church at Tompkins Avenue at McDonough Street in Bedford-Stuyvesant and relocated to its property. In March 1980, more than a hundred years after the A.M.E. Zion Church of Williamsburgh defaulted on its lease and lost its house of worship, the First A.M.E. Zion Church successfully paid off its final $54,000 mortgage payment, after which church officials burned the mortgage documents in celebration.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Materials in this collection include mortgages, receipts and financial statements, miscellaneous legal documents, internal church documents, and correspondence. Most of the materials concern the Church's financial instability and reflect debts owed by the church and transfers of its property. The materials document African American church history in Brooklyn and offer evidence of early financial and business dealings within Brooklyn's free African American community. The collection contains many documents signed by church officials and other legal authorities. Individuals whose names and/or autographs figure in this collection include: Oliver Fields, Peter Lee, Warren Mitchell, William Mitchell, Benjamin Portland, Lemuel Richardson, John G. Spence, Eugene Valentine, Major West, Thomas Wilson, and Thomas Worlds.

odd.head: General
odd.p: This file consists of a series of complex mortgages entered into by officials of the A.M.E. Zion Church concerning church property. These documents illustrate the financial instability of the church and the struggles of church administrators to retain control over their institution. Many of the documents reflect incremental payments made by the church on properties as well as their eventual default on the properties and contain multiple signatures or marks of church officials.

odd.head: General
odd.p: Includes detailed receipts and financial statements relating to the purchase and transfer of church property, the earliest dating back to 1836, just after the congregation was organized. One item is an 1853 receipt from the Brooklyn Daily Eagle, on the newspaper's letterhead.

odd.head: General
odd.p: This file consists of miscellaneous legal papers (such as depositions, official court statements, deeds, and foreclosures) that document the financial and legal dealings of A.M.E. church officials relating to church properties.

odd.head: General
odd.p: This file consists of dated lists of A.M.E. Trustees and proceedings of elections for church officers. Some documents include signatures or marks of church officials.

odd.head: General
odd.p: One letter in which Warren Mitchell inquires as to the status of foreclosure proceedings regarding the A.M.E. church property.
